title: Assess the quality of apricots for export

lessons.title: The apricot export industry, terminology and requirements
lessons.html:
Background and structure

Apricots are one of South Africa's earliest stone fruits each season. Production is mainly in the Western Cape, especially the Klein Karoo around Oudtshoorn and Calitzdorp, the Ceres area and the Breede River valley. Much of the crop goes to drying and canning, while a smaller premium share is exported fresh, mainly to Europe, the UK and the Middle East. Being early, fresh export apricots fill a window when Northern Hemisphere supply is low, which can earn good prices.

Apricot growers fall under Hortgro (stone fruit), which supports research, market access and statistics. The chain includes growers, packhouses, cold stores, exporters, shipping or air freight, and importers. Because apricots are very soft and short-lived, some are airfreighted, but most fresh exports still travel by sea in reefer containers.

Key terminology

  • Ground colour: the background skin colour, a major maturity indicator; green ground colour means immature fruit.
  • Blush: red overcolour on some cultivars.
  • Firmness: measured with a penetrometer; soft fruit will not survive transport.
  • TSS: total soluble solids or sugar content, measured in degrees Brix.
  • Split pit / split stone: a cracked stone that can let in decay.
  • Gel breakdown and internal browning: internal disorders after cold storage.
  • Class and count: quality grade and number or size of fruit per pack.

Legislative and logistical requirements

Fresh apricots for export are regulated under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990, which sets class, size, packing and marking requirements, and PPECB inspects consignments under that Act. The PPECB Act 9 of 1983 governs cold chain control. Importing countries may require a phytosanitary certificate and registration of orchards and packhouses, plus specific pest controls, for example for fruit fly.

Logistically, apricots must move quickly: harvest in the cool morning, deliver to the packhouse promptly, cool fast, pack and dispatch with minimal waiting. The exporter must book container space early, ensure correct documents and registration codes on cartons, and match the consignment to the market's protocol.

lessons.title: Sampling and assessing external and internal quality
lessons.html:
Selecting a representative sample

  • Use the sample size given in the export standards for the consignment size.
  • Select cartons at random from different pallets and from top, middle and bottom positions.
  • Handle apricots gently; rough handling during inspection itself causes bruises.
  • Record pallet and carton identification for traceability.

External quality

Check each fruit in the sample cartons for:

  • Size and uniformity within the declared range.
  • Ground colour against the colour chart: fruit must have reached the minimum maturity colour but should not be overripe.
  • Shape and suture: typical shape; uneven or swollen sutures may be limited by class.
  • Skin defects: bruises, wind and limb rub, hail damage, sunburn, cracks, healed and fresh wounds.
  • Pests and diseases: fruit fly stings, thrips damage, scale, and decay such as brown rot.
  • Stem cavity: tears around the stem allow rot.
  • Packing: correct count, fill and pad or tray placement so fruit cannot move and bruise.

Internal quality

Cut the required number of fruit and record:

  • Firmness using a penetrometer with the correct tip on peeled cheeks.
  • TSS using a calibrated refractometer on juice from the flesh.
  • Flesh condition: gel breakdown (glassy, translucent flesh), internal browning, mealiness and stone-related problems such as split pits.
  • Insect larvae in the flesh, which is a serious finding.

Apricots are delicate and mature quickly on the tree. A block harvested too early may have good firmness but low TSS and green ground colour; harvested too late, it may be soft and prone to breakdown in storage. Your job is to report the facts accurately so the right decision is made, not to guess.

lessons.title: Cold chain monitoring and the outcome of assessment
lessons.html:
Cold chain for apricots

Apricots are climacteric and have a short storage life even under ideal conditions. Delays at warm temperatures quickly cause softening and decay. Good cold chain practice includes:

  • picking in the cool part of the day and shading picked fruit in the orchard;
  • rapid cooling at the packhouse, often with forced-air cooling;
  • holding fruit at the temperature regime approved for the cultivar and market, without fluctuation;
  • keeping relative humidity high to limit shrivel;
  • quick transfer from cold store to truck to port with no standing on hot docks.

Stone fruit, including some apricot cultivars, can develop chilling-related internal disorders if held in the wrong temperature band for too long. That is why exporters follow regimes developed through industry research, and why you must check that the actual temperatures match the specified regime.

What the assessor checks

  • Pulp temperature of sample fruit with a calibrated probe.
  • Cold store temperature records and container set point against the instruction.
  • Placement of data loggers in the container.
  • Container condition and pre-cooling before loading.

Determining the outcome for the consignment

  1. Calculate defect percentages and average internal readings from your sample.
  2. Compare them with the tolerances for the declared class and with any client specification.
  3. Decide: pass for the declared class, downgrade to a lower class where allowed, or reject for that market.
  4. Record the decision and reasons on the inspection report and communicate it to the exporter.

Serious findings such as live quarantine pests or larvae in fruit, decay above tolerance, or fruit that is too soft to survive the voyage normally lead to rejection for the market. Rejected fruit may be re-sorted and re-presented if the rules allow, or sold on the local market or to processors.

Key points

  • Apricots are an early, delicate stone fruit with a short storage life.
  • Ground colour, firmness and TSS are key maturity measures.
  • Sample cartons at random across pallets and handle fruit gently.
  • Fast cooling and an approved temperature regime protect quality.
  • The assessor decides pass, downgrade or reject and records the reasons.
